factual_claims.text: A single plutonium core at Los Alamos caused two separate fatal criticality accidents nine months apart.
In August 1945 Harry Daghlian was stacking tungsten carbide bricks around the core as a neutron reflector when he dropped one onto the assembly.
Daghlian died twenty-five days after his accident.
In May 1946 Louis Slotin held two beryllium hemispheres apart with a screwdriver blade during a demonstration.

segments.narration: One plutonium sphere killed two scientists in nine months. Los Alamos had cast it for a third atomic bomb that Japan's surrender cancelled.
August 1945. Harry Daghlian stacked tungsten carbide bricks around the core, bouncing neutrons back in. He fumbled the last brick.
Blue light filled the room. He tore the brick away by hand and died twenty-five days later. The core stayed on that table.
May 1946. Louis Slotin ran a similar demonstration, holding two beryllium halves apart with a screwdriver blade.
It slipped. Slotin flipped the shell off, died nine days later, and remote handling became mandatory. The core itself was melted down.

research.summary: The demon core was a 6.2 kg plutonium sphere at Los Alamos, cast for a third atomic bomb that Japan's surrender made unnecessary. It caused two fatal criticality accidents: Harry Daghlian on 21 August 1945, after dropping a tungsten carbide reflector brick onto the assembly, who died 25 days later; and Louis Slotin on 21 May 1946, when a screwdriver holding beryllium hemispheres apart slipped, who died nine days later on 30 May. After Slotin's death criticality experiments at Los Alamos were conducted remotely, and the core was subsequently melted down and its material recycled.

segments.narration: For five days Londoners could not see their own feet. In the Isle of Dogs that was literal, in the middle of the day.
It began on Friday the fifth of December, 1952, and it did not lift until the following Tuesday.
An anticyclone had parked a lid of warm air over the city, pinning the cold, filthy air underneath it.
And the city was burning nutty slack: cheap, sulphurous coal, in every grate. The smoke had nowhere at all to go.
Four thousand deaths were counted at the time. Later work puts it near twelve thousand. Britain passed the Clean Air Act four years later.

research.summary: The Great Smog of London ran from Friday 5 December to Tuesday 9 December 1952. An anticyclone that settled over London on 4 December produced a temperature inversion, trapping cool stagnant air and the smoke of hundreds of thousands of domestic coal fires beneath a layer of warmer air. Post-war domestic coal was largely a low-grade sulphurous grade known as nutty slack, which raised sulphur dioxide output. Visibility collapsed; in the Isle of Dogs people reported being unable to see their feet. About 4,000 deaths were attributed to it at the time, and later analysis of death rates through March 1953 puts the toll between 10,000 and 12,000. The Clean Air Acts of 1956 and 1968 followed.

segments.narration: Thirty-three thousand people lived on six acres. That is Hong Kong's Kowloon Walled City, counted in a government survey in 1987.
It started as a Qing dynasty fort. Britain's 1898 lease deliberately left it out, and China never took it back.
So it grew with no architects and no permits, each block leaning on the next until the whole mass simply fused together.
It stopped at fourteen storeys for one reason: planes came in low overhead to land at Kai Tak.
Demolition ran from March 1993 to April 1994. The ground it stood on is a quiet public park now, mapped where the alleys were.

A 1987 government survey counted roughly 33,000 residents on about 2.6 hectares (6.4 acres), a density near 1.25 million people per square kilometre. It originated as a Qing military fort and was explicitly excluded from the 1898 British lease of the New Territories, leaving both governments unwilling to administer it. Buildings went up without architects or permits and were limited to roughly 13-14 storeys by the flight path into Kai Tak airport. Demolition began in March 1993 and finished in April 1994; Kowloon Walled City Park opened on the site in December 1995.

segments.narration: Miners broke into a cave of crystals bigger than trees. April 2000, three hundred metres under Chihuahua, in northern Mexico.

Inside lay beams of stone. The largest is 11.4 metres long and weighs roughly twelve tonnes. So why did they stop growing?

research.summary: The Cave of the Crystals at Naica, Chihuahua, Mexico, was exposed in April 2000 by miners excavating a new tunnel, made accessible only because the working silver and lead mine's pumps had drawn down the groundwater. Air temperatures reach 58 degrees Celsius at 90-99 percent humidity, limiting unprotected human endurance to roughly ten minutes. When mining ceased the caves were allowed to reflood in October 2015.

The body was released off Huelva, Spain at 4:15 am on 30 April 1943 carrying letters implying the Allies would strike Greece and the Balkans, with Sicily as a cover target. research.summary: A coal seam fire beneath Centralia, Pennsylvania has burned since at least 27 May 1962. Its original cause is still debated, but the best-documented account has the town council burning the landfill that day, with the fire reaching the underlying anthracite workings through an unsealed pit. Over the following decades subsidence, heat and carbon monoxide made the borough unsafe; in 1981 a sinkhole 1.2 m wide and 46 m deep opened beneath twelve-year-old Todd Domboski, who was pulled clear by his 14-year-old cousin Eric Wolfgang. Congress allocated more than $42 million for relocation in 1984, and in 1992 Governor Bob Casey invoked eminent domain over every property in the borough. At current rates the fire could burn for more than 250 years.

research.summary: The Isdal Woman's badly burned body was found on 29 November 1970 in Isdalen valley near Bergen, Norway, her face unrecognisable. All identifying labels and marks had been deliberately removed from her clothing and possessions. Two suitcases were later recovered at Bergen railway station containing clothing, wigs, makeup, currency from several countries, maps and timetables, again stripped of identification, plus a coded notebook which police decoded into an itinerary of her travels. She had used at least eight aliases and fake passports, consistently claiming Belgian nationality while completing forms in German or French. Isotope analysis of her teeth in 2017 indicated she was born around 1930, plus or minus four years, in or near Nuremberg. Norwegian authorities concluded suicide by barbiturate overdose; others argue for murder. The case remains officially unsolved.

research.summary: A rat king is a collection of rats, or mice, whose tails have become intertwined and bound together. Multiple specimens are held in European museums; the largest well-documented one, 32 rats, was discovered in 1828 in a miller's fireplace at Buchheim and is preserved at the Mauritianum in Altenburg, Germany. The binding is attributed to sticky or freezing materials such as sebum, sap, food or faeces solidifying while the animals cluster for warmth in winter. X-ray study of the 1963 Rucphen specimen confirmed callus formation at tail fractures, indicating the animals survived for an extended period while tangled. The term originally referred metaphorically to a person who exploited others, later to a king sitting on a throne of knotted tails; an alternative etymology derives it from the French rouet de rats. A living 13-rat specimen found in Estonia in 2021 confirmed the phenomenon is genuine though extremely rare.
